Description: explicit — omitted glyphs field, text renders in wrong font
prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR *When a style **does not** have a `glyphs` URL, MapLibre GL JS (v5.11 +)** automatically falls back to “local-font mode”.* Your `text-font` array is treated exactly like a CSS `font-family` list: the engine looks for a matching **web-font** (via `@font-face`) or a **system font** that exists on the client device. If the named font isn’t available, the browser picks its own generic fallback (usually *sans-serif*), which is why you see a “generic” look. This is **expected behavior**, not a bug. Below is a step-by-step explanation of what’s happening, why you see the generic font, and what you can do to get the exact font you want – either by staying in local-font mode or by switching back to the classic glyph-PBF workflow. --- ## 1. What MapLibre GL JS does when `glyphs` is missing | Version | Behaviour when `glyphs` is omitted or a glyph PBF fails | |---------|--------------------------------------------------------| | **< 5.11** | The style is considered *invalid* – the map will log an error and the text layer will be invisible. | | **≥ 5.11** | The engine **does not treat it as an error**. Instead it enters *local-font fallback mode* (see PR #4564). The `text-font` list is resolved **exactly like a CSS `font-family`** list. | ### The two code paths that end up in the same result | Situation | What MapLibre does | |-----------|--------------------| | **`glyphs` omitted** (your case) | No glyph server is consulted. For every code-point it tries to rasterise the character locally with **TinySDF** using the first available font from the `text-font` list. | | **`glyphs` present but a specific `{range}.pbf` cannot be fetched** | The same TinySDF local-render path is taken *only for the missing range*. The rest of the text may still come from the glyph server. | Both paths produce **visible text** (so the map does not break) but the visual appearance depends entirely on the fonts that the browser can actually use. --- ## 2. Why you see a “generic” font 1. **The font name you wrote in `text-font` does not match any loaded web-font** (via `@font-face`) **or any system font** on the client. * Example: `["MyCustomFont Regular"]` but you never added a `@font-face` rule for `"MyCustomFont Regular"`. 2. The browser falls back to its **default sans-serif family** (or whatever its OS-level generic fallback is). * On Windows you’ll get *Segoe UI*, on macOS *Helvetica Neue*, on Linux *Ubuntu* or *DejaVu Sans*, etc. 3. Because the fallback is **environment-dependent**, the same style can look different on different devices – exactly what you’re observing. > **Bottom line:** The map is working as designed; it is simply using whatever font the browser can find. --- ## 3. How to get the *exact* font you want You have **three main options**. Choose the one that best fits your deployment constraints (offline, CDN, branding, etc.). ### 3.1. Stay in local-font mode – load the font yourself 1. **Add a `@font-face` rule** (or use a `` that pulls a web-font) that defines the exact family name you use in `text-font`. ```css @font-face { font-family: "MyCustomFont Regular"; src: url("/fonts/MyCustomFont-Regular.woff2") format("woff2"); font-weight: normal; font-style: normal; } ``` 2. **Make sure the name matches exactly** (including spaces, case, and any weight suffix you use in the style). Example style snippet: ```json { "type": "symbol", "layout": { "text-field": "{name}", "text-font": ["MyCustomFont Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"], "text-size": 14 } } ``` 3. **Optional – preload the font** so the map doesn’t flash with the generic fallback while the font is downloading: ```js document.fonts.load('14px "MyCustomFont Regular"'); ``` 4. **Test** on a clean browser (incognito, no cache) to verify the font is being used. > **Result:** The map will render with your custom font *without* any glyph server. This works offline (as long as the font files are bundled with your app) and is the simplest way if you only need a few brand fonts. ### 3.2. Switch back to the classic glyph-PBF workflow If you prefer the **SDF-based, resolution-independent rendering** that MapLibre originally used (or you need the same look on MapLibre Native), add a `glyphs` URL and serve the appropriate PBFs. 1. **Pick a source** * **Public demo server** – `https://demotiles.maplibre.org/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf` (good for prototyping). * **OpenMapTiles fonts** – clone and host the tree yourself. * **UNDP-Data fonts** – similar, pre-packaged glyph PBFs. 2. **Add the `glyphs` field to your style JSON** (top-level, sibling of `sources` and `layers`): ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "https://my.cdn.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "sources": { … }, "layers": [ … ] } ``` 3. **Make sure the folder names match the font names** you use in `text-font`. *If you use `"MyCustomFont Regular"` you need a folder `MyCustomFont%20Regular/` (URL-escaped spaces) containing the range PBFs.* 4. **CORS** – the glyph server must send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your origin) so the browser can fetch the PBFs. 5. **Deploy** – once the URL is reachable, the map will request glyph ranges on-the-fly and render with the SDF glyphs. The appearance will be identical on GL JS and Native (provided you also configure `font-faces` on Native). > **Result:** You get the classic, resolution-independent rendering and cross-platform parity, at the cost of hosting the glyph files (or relying on a third-party server). ### 3.3. Hybrid: use glyphs for scripts that need shaping, local fonts for the rest - **CJK** (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) – by default GL JS renders these locally via `localIdeographFontFamily`. *If you *do* want to serve CJK glyphs (e.g., for a very specific typeface), set `localIdeographFontFamily: false` in the map options and provide the CJK font via `glyphs`. This is slower and usually unnecessary.* - **Latin + other scripts** – you can keep `glyphs` for those and rely on the local fallback for CJK, saving a lot of glyph-range requests. ```js const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: 'style.json', localIdeographFontFamily: false // serve CJK from glyphs (optional) }); ``` --- ## 4. What to do for **MapLibre Native** (Android / iOS) Native **does not** support the “omit `glyphs` → local-font fallback” behaviour. If you need offline rendering on Native you must: 1. **Provide a `glyphs` URL** (same as GL JS) **or** 2. **Use the `font-faces` property** (available from Android 11.13.0 / iOS 6.18.0) to map each `text-font` name to a local font file **and** an explicit Unicode range. ```json { "font-faces": [ { "font-family": "MyCustomFont Regular", "src": ["file:///android_asset/fonts/MyCustomFont-Regular.ttf"], "unicode-range": "U+0000-00FF" } ] } ``` > **Important:** `font-faces` is **not** understood by GL JS, and the `glyphs` field is still required for GL JS if you want the same look on both platforms. --- ## 5. Quick checklist – is everything set up correctly? | ✅ | Check | |---|-------| | **Font is loaded** | `@font-face` rule present **or** glyph PBFs reachable. | | **Name matches** | The string in `text-font` exactly equals the `font-family` name (including spaces, case). | | **CORS** | Glyph server returns `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for the domain. | | **GL JS version** | ≥ 5.11.0 (local-font fallback only works from this version). | | **Native compatibility** | If you need the same look on Native, add a `glyphs` URL or `font-faces`. | | **RTL / shaping** | For Arabic/Hebrew, call `setRTLTextPlugin` (see below). | | **CJK** | Either rely on the default local rendering (`localIdeographFontFamily`) or explicitly disable it if you want served glyphs. | --- ## 6. Example – fully working local-font style **style.json** ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "", // omitted on purpose – we use local fonts "sources": { "osm": { "type": "vector", "url": "https://.../tiles.json" } }, "layers": [ { "id": "place-labels", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "layout": { "text-field": "{name}", "text-font": ["MyBrand Bold", "Noto Sans Regular"], "text-size": 14, "text-anchor": "center" }, "paint": { "text-color": "#222" } } ] } ``` **HTML / CSS** ```html
``` **CSS (font-face)** ```css @font-face { font-family: "MyBrand Bold"; src: url("/fonts/MyBrand-Bold.woff2") format("woff2"); font-weight: bold; font-style: normal; } ``` Result: Labels appear in *MyBrand Bold* on every device, no glyph server needed. --- ## 7. RTL & shaping reminder (Arabic, Hebrew, etc.) Even when the correct font is loaded, **right-to-left scripts need the RTL plugin**: ```js import { setRTLTextPlugin } from 'maplibre-gl'; setRTLTextPlugin( 'https://unpkg.com/maplibre-gl/dist/maplibre-gl-rtl-text.js', null, true // defer loading until needed ); ``` Call this **before** you instantiate the map. Without it, Arabic/Hebrew will appear left-to-right and the glyphs will look wrong. --- ## 8. Bottom line - **Not a bug** – MapLibre GL JS is deliberately falling back to the browser’s local fonts when `glyphs` is missing. - The generic font you see is the browser’s fallback because the named font isn’t available locally. - **Fixes:** 1. Load the desired font as a web-font (`@font-face`) **or** 2. Add a proper `glyphs` URL and serve the matching PBFs (or both, if you need cross-platform parity). Pick the approach that matches your project’s needs (offline-first branding vs. cross-platform SDF rendering). If you later need the same look on MapLibre Native, remember that Native still requires either a glyph server **or** the `font-faces` property; the GL JS omit-`glyphs` shortcut will not work there.

Description: implicit — offline/local fonts on MapLibre Native, not GL JS
prompt: I'm building an offline map app with MapLibre Native on Android and want labels to render in local device fonts without running a glyphs server. What's the right way to configure this?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## TL;DR **MapLibre Native (Android) → local-font rendering = `font-faces` property** 1. **Package the TTF/OTF files** you want to use (e.g. Noto Sans, Noto Sans Arabic, Noto Sans CJK SC) into the app’s `assets/` folder. 2. **Add a `font-faces` array** to the style JSON (or to a separate “font-faces” JSON that you merge at runtime). Each entry maps a *font-stack name* (the value you will write in `text-font`) to one or more local font files **and** the Unicode ranges that those files cover. 3. **Reference the same font-stack name** in every `symbol` layer’s `text-font` (fallback list works the same as in GL JS). 4. **No `glyphs` field** (or set it to an empty string) – the native SDK will never try to fetch glyph PBFs; it will read the glyphs directly from the bundled fonts. 5. **CJK caveat** – Native does **not** have the GL JS “local-ideograph” shortcut yet, so you must still provide glyph PBFs for CJK if you need them, or accept that those characters will be missing. 6. **RTL scripts** – load the RTL text plugin (only needed for GL JS; Native already uses HarfBuzz for shaping when you supply a font that contains the needed glyphs). Below is a complete, step-by-step guide, plus a minimal working example. --- ## 1. Put the font files in your APK ``` app/ └─ src/ └─ main/ └─ assets/ └─ fonts/ ├─ NotoSans-Regular.ttf ├─ NotoSans-Bold.ttf ├─ NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf ├─ NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf ← optional, see CJK note └─ ... (any other custom fonts) ``` *Tip:* Keep the files under `assets/fonts/` (or any sub-folder you like) – you’ll reference them with a relative path later. --- ## 2. Create the `font-faces` section The `font-faces` property lives **outside** the normal `sources`, `layers`, `sprite`, etc. It is a top-level array of objects: ```json { "version": 8, "name": "Offline demo", "glyphs": "", // ← empty – we never use a glyph server "font-faces": [ { "font-family": "Noto Sans Regular", "src": "asset://fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": "U+0000-00FF, U+0100-024F, U+0250-02AF" }, { "font-family": "Noto Sans Bold", "src": "asset://fonts/NotoSans-Bold.ttf", "unicode-range": "U+0000-00FF, U+0100-024F, U+0250-02AF" }, { "font-family": "Noto Sans Arabic Regular", "src": "asset://fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": "U+0600-06FF, U+0750-077F, U+08A0-08FF" }, { "font-family": "Noto Sans CJK SC Regular", "src": "asset://fonts/NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf", "unicode-range": "U+4E00-9FFF, U+3400-4DBF, U+20000-2A6DF" } ], "layers": [ … ] } ``` ### Field meanings | Field | Required? | What to put | |-------|-----------|-------------| | `font-family` | ✅ | The exact string you will later use in `text-font`. It can contain spaces; just keep it identical. | | `src` | ✅ | A URI that the native SDK can resolve. `asset://` tells the SDK to load the file from the APK’s assets. You can also use `file://` for an external storage path, or `http://`/`https://` for a remote font (still offline-friendly if you ship it locally). | | `unicode-range` | ✅ | A comma-separated list of Unicode ranges that this file covers. **Only the ranges you list will be used**; any codepoint outside will fall back to the next entry in the `text-font` list (or become invisible if none match). Use the `U+xxxx-xxxx` syntax exactly as shown. | | `weight` (optional) | ❌ | If you want to expose a weight keyword (`"bold"`), you can add `"weight": 700`. The SDK will treat the entry as a weight-specific face. | | `style` (optional) | ❌ | `"style": "italic"` for italic faces. | > **Why the explicit `unicode-range`?** > Native does not have a shaping engine that can decide “which font covers this glyph”. It simply looks up the first `font-face` whose range includes the codepoint. Supplying the ranges guarantees deterministic fallback and keeps the lookup fast. ### Generating the ranges automatically If you are unsure which ranges a font covers, you can extract them with a small Node script using the `unicode-range` npm package, or with `ttx` (part of FontTools) and grep the `` table. For most Noto fonts the ranges are documented in the Noto GitHub repo; copy-paste them. --- ## 3. Use the font-stack in your style layers ```json { "id": "place-labels", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], "text-font": [ "Noto Sans Bold", // primary – Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, etc. "Noto Sans Arabic Regular", // fallback for Arabic "Noto Sans CJK SC Regular" // fallback for Chinese (if you supplied it) ], "text-size": 14 }, "paint": { "text-color": "#222" } } ``` *The order matters*: the first entry that contains the needed glyph wins. If a codepoint is not covered by any of the listed faces, the label will be invisible. --- ## 4. Load the style in your Android code ```kotlin val mapView = findViewById(R.id.mapView) val styleJson = assets.open("style/offline-style.json") .bufferedReader() .use { it.readText() } mapView.getMapboxMap().loadStyleJson(styleJson) { // style is ready – you can now add sources, layers, etc. } ``` No extra configuration is needed; the native SDK automatically parses the `font-faces` array, registers the fonts with its internal `FontManager`, and uses them when rendering `symbol` layers. --- ## 5. CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) – what you need to know | Platform | Default behavior | What you must do for offline | |----------|------------------|------------------------------| | **MapLibre GL JS (≥ 5.11)** | `localIdeographFontFamily` generates CJK glyphs on-device (TinySDF) – no glyph server needed. | Nothing extra; you can optionally set `localIdeographFontFamily` to a nicer system font. | | **MapLibre Native (Android / iOS)** | **No local-ideograph shortcut** – the engine always expects glyph PBFs for CJK ranges. | **Option 1:** Ship a *glyph server* (e.g. a tiny HTTP server inside the app) that serves the standard Noto CJK PBFs.
**Option 2:** Accept missing CJK characters (they will be invisible).
**Option 3:** Use a *fallback bitmap* approach (render the text to a bitmap yourself and add it as an `icon-image`), but that defeats the purpose of vector labels. | If you decide to go with option 1, the easiest path is to copy the pre-built Noto CJK glyph PBF tree from the OpenMapTiles `fonts` repo into your assets and point `glyphs` at `asset://fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`. The same `font-faces` entries above are **not** needed for CJK in that case; the engine will read the PBFs. --- ## 6. RTL scripts (Arabic, Hebrew, Syriac, etc.) MapLibre Native already uses HarfBuzz for shaping when a font that contains the required glyphs is supplied via `font-faces`. No extra plugin is required (the GL JS `setRTLTextPlugin` call is GL-only). Just make sure: * The font you bundle includes the proper Arabic/Hebrew glyphs **and** the OpenType tables for shaping (Noto Sans Arabic does). * The `unicode-range` you declare covers the Arabic block (`U+0600-06FF` etc.). If you see characters displayed left-to-right or with missing ligatures, double-check that the font file is not a “subset” that stripped the shaping tables. --- ## 7. Full minimal example (assets + code) ### Directory layout ``` app/ └─ src/ └─ main/ ├─ assets/ │ ├─ style/ │ │ └─ offline-style.json │ └─ fonts/ │ ├─ NotoSans-Regular.ttf │ ├─ NotoSans-Bold.ttf │ ├─ NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf │ └─ NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf ← optional └─ java/com/example/offlinemap/MainActivity.kt ``` ### `offline-style.json` ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "", // <-- important: no remote glyph server "font-faces": [ { "font-family": "Noto Sans Regular", "src": "asset://fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": "U+0000-00FF, U+0100-024F, U+0250-02AF" }, { "font-family": "Noto Sans Bold", "src": "asset://fonts/NotoSans-Bold.ttf", "unicode-range": "U+0000-00FF, U+0100-024F, U+0250-02AF" }, { "font-family": "Noto Sans Arabic Regular", "src": "asset://fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": "U+0600-06FF, U+0750-077F, U+08A0-08FF" }, { "font-family": "Noto Sans CJK SC Regular", "src": "asset://fonts/NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf", "unicode-range": "U+4E00-9FFF, U+3400-4DBF, U+20000-2A6DF" } ], "sources": { "osm": { "type": "vector", "url": "asset://tiles/tileset.json" } }, "layers": [ { "id": "water", "type": "fill", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "water", "paint": { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" } }, { "id": "place-labels", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], "text-font": [ "Noto Sans Bold", "Noto Sans Arabic Regular", "Noto Sans CJK SC Regular" ], "text-size": 14, "text-anchor": "center" }, "paint": { "text-color": "#222" } } ] } ``` ### `MainActivity.kt` ```kotlin class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() { private lateinit var mapView: MapView override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) { super.onCreate(savedInstanceState) setContentView(R.layout.activity_main) mapView = findViewById(R.id.mapView) // Load the style JSON from assets val styleJson = assets.open("style/offline-style.json") .bufferedReader() .use { it.readText() } mapView.getMapboxMap().loadStyleJson(styleJson) { // Optional: add any runtime sources / layers here } // If you have a custom tile source, make sure its URL also uses the // "asset://" scheme or a local file path. } override fun onStart() { super.onStart() mapView.onStart() } override fun onStop() { super.onStop() mapView.onStop() } // … (other lifecycle callbacks) } ```
